messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mika is a 42-year-old electrician of Pacific Islander background who came to treatment after more than a year of living as though danger could break through an ordinary day without warning. The assault happened at dusk, near the end of a long job. He had been locking up a small commercial site when he heard a door bang behind him and turned too late. What he remembers most clearly are a few sharp pictures: the door swinging open, a man stepping fast into his space, a flash of a raised arm, the concrete coming up toward him. The rest is broken and missing. He cannot put the event into a full sequence, only return to isolated moments that arrive with a physical jolt, and whenever they do he is flooded with guilt, convinced he should have seen it coming or handled it differently.

In the weeks after, dusk became the hardest part of the day. As the light starts to change, Mika feels his body tighten before he has consciously thought about why. The sound of a door opening sharply at a worksite, or slamming in a store, can pull up one of those frozen images so abruptly that for a moment he feels detached and unreal, as if he is no longer fully in the present. In those moments he does not just remember the assault; he lands again in the belief that it says something shameful about him. He has come to believe the attack happened because of the kind of man he is—careless, weak, the sort of person who ends up in that situation when someone better would not have. By evening, especially at the same time of day it happened, his thoughts darken quickly into the sense that nothing ahead of him is likely to improve.

Those meanings have made him live as if vulnerability is visible on him. At work, if someone moves suddenly in the edge of his vision, he jerks back as though bracing for another blow. If a coworker touches his shoulder without warning, he reacts with instant alarm and then embarrassment. He avoids unfamiliar buildings whenever he can, telling himself he needs to know exits and blind spots before he can relax, but underneath is a conviction that he is the kind of person things happen to. The broken, snapshot quality of the memory keeps that danger feeling alive; because he cannot fill in what happened between the fragments, he treats what he cannot remember as further evidence that he was overwhelmed and failed.

Mika has built his evenings around not having to think. When dusk approaches, or when a door bangs and leaves him briefly unreal and shaky, he buries himself in his phone for hours, scrolling, gaming, clicking through anything that can keep his mind occupied. On worse nights he drinks until he feels dulled enough not to see the pictures so vividly. He has stopped watching films or shows with assaults or tense confrontations because he knows how quickly they can set him off. The same happens when the memory intrudes on its own: once the images start, and the guilt comes with them, he reaches for a screen or alcohol to push them away.

These habits have narrowed his life and deepened the conclusions he draws about himself. He is less present with his partner in the evenings, sitting beside her but absorbed in his phone or drinking past conversation. He feels ashamed of how much time disappears this way, and that shame confirms his hopelessness: in his mind, a man who has to manage himself like this is not someone with much of a future. The drinking and constant distraction also leave him less grounded, so the next day he is more keyed up, more likely to react to sudden movement or touch, and more dependent on scanning whether a place feels safe enough to enter.

Over time, the strategies meant to keep the assault out of mind have made the triggers more central in his life. He organizes routes and jobs to avoid unfamiliar places, but that means doors slamming at the sites he does attend, and the approach of dusk on every workday, stand out even more. He notices the time constantly. He has begun to dread the first hint of feeling detached, because he takes that sensation itself as a sign that he is slipping back toward the assault and toward those same accusing thoughts about what sort of person he is. When he finally sought help, it was after snapping away from a coworker who touched him unexpectedly and then sitting in his truck after work, unable to face going into another building. What frightened him most was the sense that his world was shrinking around a handful of moments he could not fully remember, and what he hopes for is simple: to get through the end of the day without feeling that the assault is still waiting for him.
